text:
Round three. What would a crash do to the portfolios people actually own today?

I split the world index into four buckets. The AI giants, about twenty-five percent. The rest of the US, about forty-six. Other developed markets, about twenty-nine. And for global funds, emerging markets.

Then I ran two scenarios, based on what really happened in past crashes. These are scenarios, not forecasts.

Scenario A: the AI giants fall fifty percent, the rest of the US ten, other developed markets five, emerging markets fifteen.

Scenario B is a full dot-com replay. The AI giants lose seventy percent, the rest of the US thirty-five, other developed markets forty, emerging markets forty-five.

That isn't made up. From 2000 to 2002, the big tech names of that era lost seventy to ninety percent, the S and P five hundred about half, and Europe about two thirds.

The maths is simple: each portfolio's weight in each bucket, times that bucket's loss, added up. You could redo it on a napkin.

Scenario A first. A plain M S C I World ETF loses about eighteen and a half percent.

Switch to an All-World fund with emerging markets, and you get to minus eighteen point two. Almost no difference.

Because emerging markets are full of AI too. Taiwan and Korea are home to some of the biggest chipmakers on the planet.

An equal weight world fund, where every company gets the same slice, loses only seven percent. The AI giants are less than one percent of it.

Europe only looks safe in this scenario, but Europe has its own giants. A few companies like A S M L, S A P and Novo Nordisk drive a big part of its returns. Concentration isn't only American.

Europe only: minus five. And a sixty forty portfolio with euro government bonds: minus nine.

In an AI-only correction, the alternatives really work. Now, scenario B.

M S C I World, minus forty-five. All-World, also minus forty-five.

Equal weight, minus thirty-eight. Europe only, minus forty. And the sixty forty, minus twenty-four.

This is the uncomfortable result. In a real crash, swapping one stock index for another barely matters.

In money: on a one hundred thousand euro portfolio, scenario B takes about forty-five thousand from a world ETF, thirty-eight thousand from equal weight, and twenty-four thousand from a sixty forty.

The only thing that really changed the outcome was owning something that isn't stocks.

That doesn't make equal weight or All-World bad ideas. Since 2000, equal weight even edged out the standard index, about seven point eight percent a year versus seven point five, in dollars. They're just not crash protection.
